lesson.title: The Power That Counts: The Watt as a Unit of Real Power
lesson.summary: The watt is the SI unit of real power, the portion of AC (or DC) power that is actually converted into heat, light, motion, or other useful work, as opposed to the reactive power that merely oscillates without being consumed. It is the number that appears on an electric bill because it is the only power a meter actually charges for.
lesson.body:
Every watt of electrical power delivered to a load corresponds to one joule of energy converted per second into something useful: a resistor heating up, a motor turning a shaft, a light bulb glowing. In a purely resistive DC circuit, computing watts is direct Ohm's Law territory: P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R. In an AC circuit, the calculation needs one more ingredient, because voltage and current are not always perfectly in step with each other, and only the portion of current that lines up in phase with the voltage does any actual work.

That is captured in the real power formula P = V x I x cos(theta), where V and I are rms values and theta is the phase angle between voltage and current. The cos(theta) term is the power factor, and it acts like an efficiency multiplier on the raw V times I product: a purely resistive load has theta = 0, cos(theta) = 1, and all of V x I converts to real watts. A purely reactive load (an ideal inductor or capacitor alone) has theta = 90 degrees, cos(theta) = 0, and delivers zero real watts no matter how much current flows, because the current is entirely out of step with the voltage.

Return to the same load used to illustrate the VAR: 120 V rms, 10 A rms, lagging power factor 0.8, so theta = 36.87 degrees and cos(theta) = 0.8. The real power is P = V x I x cos(theta) = 120 x 10 x 0.8 = 960 W. Notice this is a smaller number than the raw V times I product of 1,200, precisely because the 0.8 power factor means only 80 percent of the apparent voltamperes actually convert into working power; the rest is the reactive power discussed under VAR, which does not register as watts at all.

A purely resistive check confirms the formula reduces correctly: if that same load were instead a 12 ohm resistor carrying 10 A rms with voltage and current perfectly in phase, P = I^2 x R = 10^2 x 12 = 1,200 W, matching V x I exactly because cos(theta) = 1 for a resistor. Comparing the two cases side by side shows exactly what the power factor costs: the reactive, lagging load only delivers 960 of the 1,200 VA the source is working to supply, while the purely resistive load delivers the full 1,200 W, which is the entire motivation behind power factor correction: raising cos(theta) closer to 1 so that more of the apparent power a utility supplies actually shows up as billable watts.

Utility meters are built to track watts (or more precisely watt-hours) rather than volt-amperes specifically because watts represent energy that was actually converted into something useful. That is also why industrial customers with poor power factor sometimes face separate reactive-power penalty charges: the utility still has to size its generators and wires for the full apparent current, even though it can only bill for the real, working watts.

It is easy to conflate watts with volt-amperes because for a resistive load the two numbers happen to be identical, but they measure fundamentally different things and only coincide when the power factor is exactly 1. Keeping that distinction sharp, real power in watts as the working output, apparent power in volt-amperes as the total electrical burden, is what makes power factor correction and equipment sizing calculations make sense rather than feeling like arbitrary unit conversions.
